text:
Marginal distribution added on X and Y axis of a scatter plot


Reference: Marginal distribution with ggplot2 and ggExtra



The data they used is mtcars.


Code
head(mtcars)


                   mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
Valiant           18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1


This graph uses two marks: points and bars.
Points

x position: wt
y position: mpg
color: cyl
size: cyl

Bar

x position & count: wt
y position & count: mpg




It shows the scatter plot of x to y as well as each x and y distributions around the scatter plot. I’m not sure what mpg and wt values represent since the website doesn’t include explanation for the data.



It is a good graphic because it shows the same information in multiple ways: overlaying a dot plot of x vs. y and two histograms for each x and y.



It seems quite simple to make the scatter plot and histogram separately. I would have to do most of the work in encoding.



Overlaying different types of marks

text:
Option A - The pie adds up to a circle, which is intuitive thinking that the numbers are percentages.
Option B - It’s easy to compare the height of the bars since they are right next to each other. Also, the bars are colored easily showing which year it’s from.
Option C - The bars are centered at the response “Agree,” which makes it easy to look at the trend.
Option D - The differences are easily conceivable looking at the slopes.



Option A - Pies are hard to compare since human eyes have trouble finding differences between shapes when they’re at different angles.
Option B - You have to make the comparison from left to right, looking at them one by one.
Option C - It is very hard to compare the “Strongly Disagree” portion without looking at the text.
Option D - Since they don’t stack, it is hard to know how the responses adds up.



Since want to show how employees responded this year compared to last year to the retention item, I want to emphasize the comparison between this year and last year. Option D does the best job demonstrating this comparison. It directly shows the difference using the slope connecting two points.



My friend said they prefer Option C because it is easier to understand the overall trend of what proportion of people responded positively or negatively.

title: hw7
text:
Always start at zero.
For long category labels, it is better two swap the x and y axis to make a horizontal bar plot.
Bars should be ordered in a meaningful way.

If the categories have no natural order, bars should be arranged by their data values (ascending/descending).
But if the categories represent ordered variable, the natural order should be kept.

For plots that display only few numbers, adding the actual numbers to the plot increases information density and removes the need for an explicit y axis.




Limitation of bar chart: they need to start at zero. It is not advised to use a bar chart when the data consists of values that are far from zero and have relatively small differences between them (e.g., life expectancy between 60 and 81 years).




Dot plots: placing dots at specific locations along an axis

They are particularly useful when the axis range needs to be limited (not starting at zero) to highlight small differences.

Heatmaps: map data values onto a color scale rather than a position scale

They are preferred for very large or complex datasets where bars or dots would make the figure too busy to identify broader trends.





Stack bars? Don’t? - Stacking is appropriate only when the sum of the individual bars represents a meaningful total amount. - Don’t stack values where the sum is not meaningful (e.g., median incomes).
Dodge - Grouped bars are used to visualize two categorical variables simultaneously. - They require the viewer to match bar colors to a legend. - Wilke prefers using small multiples (separate regular bar plots for each category) to avoid the need for color-coding and simplify comparisons.

Exercise 2 (A video presentation by Healy)

a. Watch this video starting at 12:18 until 49:52. (You are welcome to watch the whole thing if you like.) You will see some things that look familiar from our discussion of perception in class, but there are also a number of additional examples and discussion.


b. List at least three pieces of advice you can glean from this video that might help you design good graphics.

Rely on fixed baselines instead of angles or floating areas.
Design with your specific audience in mind.
Use a “layer, highlight, and repeat” strategy.



c. There are two figures in this video that come from Chapter 1 of Tufte (2001). Did you spot them? Which figures are they?
